1a.say: In this lesson you will learn the rule the SAT tests most often: how to join two complete sentences.
A complete sentence needs two things: a **subject**, who or what, and a **verb**, what happens.
Here is a second complete sentence. Again, a subject and a verb.
Now we put them side by side. What should go in the gap?
First try: only a comma. This is called a **comma splice**, and the SAT always marks it wrong.
Second try: nothing at all. The two sentences crash into each other. This is a **run-on**. Also wrong.
Option one: a **period**. Now we have two separate sentences. Correct.
Option two: a **semicolon**. It works exactly like a period, but the second sentence starts with a small letter.
Option three: a **comma plus a joining word**, such as and, but, or so.
Option four: a **colon**, when the second sentence explains the first one.
Now a trap. The second part starts with By 1900. It looks like a short extra phrase. Look closer.
After the phrase there is a subject, it, and a verb, had doubled. So this is a complete sentence, and a comma is not enough.
The same trap with an i n g phrase. Hoping for rain sounds unfinished, but the farmers waited is a full sentence.
A real SAT sentence. The left side is complete. The right side has a subject, observation, and a verb, led. Two complete sentences, so we use a period.
t: In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that mold had killed the bacteria in one of his dishes

1a.say: Remember: check the left side and the right side. Two complete sentences need a period, a semicolon, a comma with and, but, or so, or a colon.

1b.say: Some small words change everything: although, because, while, when, since, if, once, and even though.
It rained is a complete sentence.
Put although in front of it, and it is no longer complete. Although it rained... what happened? We are still waiting.
This is a **dependent clause**. It cannot stand alone. It must attach to a main clause.
When the dependent clause comes first, put a **comma** after it.
A semicolon is wrong here. A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, and the left side is not complete.
A period is wrong too. It leaves the dependent clause alone as a **fragment**.
Do not use although and but together. One joining word is enough.
When the dependent clause comes at the end, you usually need no comma at all.
Long dependent clauses work the same way. The comma goes at the very end of the clause, right before the main subject.
t: When the museum finally opened its new wing in 2019

1b.say: A common trap: the comma comes too early, in the middle of the dependent clause.
t: its new wing in 2019 visitors lined up.

1b.say: A real SAT sentence. However long the dependent clause is, it ends with only a comma.
t: Although the Atacama Desert receives less than a millimeter of rain in some years

1b.say: To sum up: dependent clause, comma, main clause. No semicolon, no period, and no extra but.

1c.say: Seven words can join two sentences with a comma. An easy way to remember them is **FANBOYS**: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.
When one of these words joins two complete sentences, the comma goes **before** it.
A comma after the joining word is wrong.
Each word shows a different relationship. And adds. But contrasts. So shows a result.
Now a trap. Here there is only **one subject** with two verbs. She studied, and she passed.
The second part, and passed, is not a complete sentence. So no comma goes before and.
Add a subject to the second part, and now you need the comma.
Another trap: however is not one of the seven words. A comma before however makes a comma splice.
Only for, and, nor, but, or, yet, and so can join two sentences with just a comma.
A real SAT sentence. Two complete sentences, joined by a comma and but.
t: The first transatlantic telegraph cable was completed in 1858
after only three weeks of service.

1c.say: Summary: two complete sentences take a comma before the joining word. One subject with two verbs takes no comma.

2a.say: The **semicolon** is a period in disguise. It needs a complete sentence on both sides.
If the right side is not a complete sentence, the semicolon is wrong.
If the left side is not complete, it is wrong too.
Here a comma is the right choice.
Now meet the **transition words**: however, therefore, moreover, for example, in fact. They are not joining words like and or but.
When a transition starts the second sentence, use a semicolon before it and a comma after it.
A comma before however creates a comma splice. This is one of the most common wrong answers.
A period also works. Then however starts a new sentence with a capital letter.
Sometimes the transition sits inside one sentence. Then it simply takes a comma on each side.
The hardest version: where does the second sentence begin? Read for meaning. Here the contrast is about the second test, so the semicolon goes after failed.
A real SAT sentence. Two complete sentences, with semicolon, therefore, comma in the middle.
t: Early cameras required subjects to remain motionless for long periods
hidden metal stands to hold heads in place.

2a.say: Summary: a semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides. Before a transition word, use semicolon, transition, comma.

2b.say: A **colon** tells the reader: here comes the explanation, or here comes the list.
Rule one: the part before the colon must be a complete sentence.
Here is a list after a colon. The left side is complete, so this is correct.
Here the left side stops in the middle. The goals were... what? It is not complete, so no colon.
Just remove the colon. The sentence flows by itself.
Never put a colon right after such as or including.
Also, no colon between a verb and its object.
Watch for signal words before a colon: threefold, two reasons, one problem, the following.
t: to learn, to practice, and to rest

2b.say: The part after a colon can also be a full sentence that explains the first one.
A real SAT sentence. The left side mentions one simple reason, and the reason comes after the colon.
t: The results surprised the research team for one simple reason
the control group, which received no treatment at all, improved the most

2b.say: Summary: complete sentence, colon, then the list or explanation. If the left side is unfinished, no colon.

2c.say: The **dash** has two jobs. Job one: a single dash works like a colon.
Just like a colon, the part before a single dash must be a complete sentence.
Job two: a **pair of dashes** works like a pair of commas. They wrap extra information.
Test it: remove the extra part. The sentence still works.
If you open with a dash, you must close with a dash, not a comma.
And if you open with a comma, close with a comma, not a dash.
On the test, find the opening mark first. Then choose the same mark to close.
The opening mark is a dash, so the closing mark is a dash.
A single dash cannot separate a subject from its verb.
A real SAT sentence. A long extra phrase opens with a dash and closes with a dash. Then the verb comes.
t: a stone mill constructed in 1792 by local farmers
a small museum of regional history.

2c.say: Summary: one dash works like a colon. Two dashes work like two commas. Always match the opening mark.

2d.say: A normal list uses commas between the items.
But what if each item already has a comma inside it?
Now the reader cannot see where one item ends. So we put **semicolons between** the items.
Commas stay inside each item. Semicolons go between the items.
Do not mix them. A semicolon in one place and a comma in another is wrong.
And a semicolon inside an item is also wrong.
The same rule works for names with descriptions.
A real SAT sentence. Every item has a comma inside, so semicolons separate the items.
t: The conference brought together scientists from

2d.say: Summary: if the items have commas inside, separate the items with semicolons.
